section.title: The Twelve Spies
section.sectionRationale: At the very edge of the promised land, twelve leaders are sent to spy out Canaan, and their divided report, ten voices of fear against Caleb's lone voice of faith, sets up the great national crisis of chapter 14, making this one of the wilderness narratives the New Testament treats as an abiding warning against unbelief, 1 Corinthians 10:1-13, Hebrews 3-4.
section.thesis: Twelve leaders see the same good and fruitful land and the same formidable inhabitants, yet ten choose to measure God's promise by the size of the obstacle while Caleb alone measures the obstacle by the size of God's promise, showing that unbelief and faith can look at identical facts and reach opposite conclusions.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the twelve leaders named and sent to spy out Canaan; Moses' specific instructions for what to observe; the spies' forty-day journey and their report of a rich but formidably defended land; and Caleb's call to go up at once against the ten spies' report of fear.

units.label: The twelve leaders sent to spy out Canaan

verses.text: And the LORD said to Moses,
“Send out for yourself men to {{spy|spy}} out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites. From each of their fathers' tribes send one man who is a leader among them.”
So at the consent of the LORD, Moses sent them out from the Wilderness of Paran. All the men were leaders of the Israelites,

and these were their names: 
From the tribe of Reuben, Shammua son of Zaccur;
from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat son of Hori;
from the tribe of Judah, Caleb son of Jephunneh;
from the tribe of Issachar, Igal son of Joseph;
from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea son of Nun;
from the tribe of Benjamin, Palti son of Raphu;
from the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel son of Sodi;
from the tribe of Manasseh, a tribe of Joseph, Gaddi son of Susi;
from the tribe of Dan, Ammiel son of Gemalli;
from the tribe of Asher, Sethur son of Michael;
from the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi son of Vophsi;
and from the tribe of Gad, Geuel son of Machi.
These were the names of the men Moses sent to spy out the land; and Moses gave to Hoshea son of Nun the name Joshua.
When Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan, he told them, “Go up through the Negev and into the hill country.
See what the land is like and whether its people are strong or weak, few or many.
Is the land where they live good or bad? Are the cities where they dwell open camps or fortifications?
Is the soil fertile or unproductive? Are there trees in it or not? Be courageous, and bring back some of the fruit of the land.” (It was the season for the first ripe grapes.)

units.label: The spies' journey and the report of the land

verses.text: So they went up and spied out the land from the Wilderness of Zin as far as Rehob, toward Lebo-hamath.
They went up through the Negev and came to Hebron, where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak, dwelled. It had been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.
When they came to the Valley of Eshcol, they cut down a branch with a single cluster of grapes, which they carried on a pole between two men. They also took some pomegranates and figs.
Because of the cluster of grapes the Israelites cut there, that place was called the Valley of Eshcol.
After forty days the men returned from spying out the land,

and they went back to Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation of Israel in the Wilderness of Paran at Kadesh. They brought back a report for the whole congregation and showed them the fruit of the land.
And they gave this account to Moses: “We went into the land to which you sent us, and indeed, it is flowing with milk and honey. Here is some of its fruit!
Nevertheless, the people living in the land are strong, and the cities are large and fortified. We even saw the descendants of Anak there.
The Amalekites live in the land of the Negev; the Hittites, Jebusites, and Amorites live in the hill country; and the Canaanites live by the sea and along the Jordan.”

units.label: Caleb's call to go up, and the ten spies' fear

verses.text: Then Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said, “We must go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly conquer it!”
But the men who had gone up with him replied, “We cannot go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are!”
So they gave the Israelites a bad report about the land that they had spied out: “The land we explored devours its inhabitants, and all the people we saw there are great in stature.
We even saw the Nephilim there, the descendants of Anak that come from the Nephilim! We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight, and we must have seemed the same to them!”

spy.gloss: To spy out, explore, or seek out. Describes the careful, deliberate scouting the twelve leaders undertook; both the fearful majority and Caleb's faithful minority saw the identical explored land, showing the decisive factor was not the evidence but the faith or fear interpreting it.

basic.context: At the border of Canaan, Moses sends twelve tribal leaders to spy out the land the LORD is giving Israel. After forty days, they return with real fruit as proof of the land's richness, but ten of the twelve report that the land's inhabitants are too strong to overcome, while Caleb alone insists Israel can certainly take the land because the LORD is with them.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing an actual reconnaissance mission and its divided report, and the New Testament treats the ensuing unbelief as a direct warning: 1 Corinthians 10:1-13 and Hebrews 3-4 use this very episode to warn believers against hardening their hearts through unbelief. The chapter itself is descriptive, showing exactly how fear distorts perception even of good and factual evidence.
basic.originalLanguages: The verb tur, to spy out or explore, describes a careful, deliberate scouting mission, not a casual glance; both the ten spies and Caleb saw the same tur, the same explored land, yet interpreted the identical facts through radically different lenses of fear and faith.
basic.typology: Caleb's minority report of faith, standing against the majority's fear despite identical evidence, anticipates the pattern of the faithful remnant throughout Scripture, and ultimately Christ, who alone perfectly trusted the Father's promises against every appearance of overwhelming opposition, even the cross itself.
basic.christ: Where the ten spies concluded we cannot despite God's explicit promise and presence, Christ is the ultimate yes to every promise of God, 2 Corinthians 1:20, trusting His Father's word completely even facing an obstacle infinitely greater than fortified cities, the cross itself, and emerging victorious exactly as promised.
basic.god: God has already promised this good land to Israel and demonstrated His power decisively in the exodus and at Sinai, yet the spies' report reveals how easily His people can let visible obstacles eclipse His spoken word. God's patience with this moment of fear-filled reporting, before the actual rebellion breaks out in chapter 14, shows Him giving space for faith to answer fear before judgment falls.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 10:1-13 warns believers directly from Israel's wilderness failures, including this episode. Hebrews 3:16-19 asks who provoked God, identifying it as those who came out of Egypt. 2 Corinthians 1:20 declares that every one of God's promises is yes in Christ. Deuteronomy 1:19-33 retells this episode from Moses' own later perspective.
basic.oneStory: Israel stands at the very border of the promised land with God's word and power already proven, yet ten leaders let fear override the promise while one, Caleb, trusts God's word against every visible obstacle. That contrast between fear and faith runs through the whole Bible and finds its resolution in Christ, in whom every promise of God is answered with a decisive yes.

context.literary:
Numbers 13 opens the hinge of the whole book. The first ten chapters arrange the camp at Sinai around the tabernacle; from Numbers 10:11 Israel is on the move, and by Numbers 12:16 they are camped in the Wilderness of Paran, a short march from the land. Chapters 13 and 14 are one story told in two panels: the mission and its report, then the people's response and God's verdict. Chapter 13 supplies the evidence; chapter 14 shows what the people do with it.

The chapter moves in four steps. A divine command and a list of twelve names, verses 1 to 16. A set of instructions arranged as paired alternatives, strong or weak, few or many, good or bad, open camps or fortifications, fertile or unproductive, verses 17 to 20. A journey summarised in one long sweep from the Wilderness of Zin to Lebo-hamath, then slowed down at two places, Hebron and the Valley of Eshcol, verses 21 to 24. And the report, verses 25 to 33, which itself escalates in three stages.

That escalation is the literary heart of the chapter. The first report, verses 27 to 29, is balanced: the land is good, here is the fruit, nevertheless the people are strong. Caleb speaks into that balance, verse 30. The ten then answer him, verse 31, and in verse 32 their account turns from a report 'to Moses' into 'a bad report' spread among 'the Israelites.' The land that flowed with milk and honey in verse 27 now 'devours its inhabitants,' and the Anakim of verse 28 have become Nephilim by verse 33. The facts have not changed between verse 27 and verse 33; the storytelling has. Moses the narrator lets the reader watch fear rewrite the evidence sentence by sentence.

Notice, too, what the chapter holds back. The LORD speaks in verses 1 and 2 and then falls silent until chapter 14. Caleb's word is the only voice in the chapter that echoes what God has already said.
context.historical:
Kadesh, verse 26, called Kadesh-barnea in Deuteronomy 1:19 and Joshua 14:6, lay in the dry country south of Canaan, on the border between the Wilderness of Paran and the Wilderness of Zin, Numbers 20:1. It was an oasis and a natural staging post. From there the spies went up 'through the Negev and into the hill country,' verse 17, the ordinary route north along the central ridge.

Their range was the whole land. The Wilderness of Zin marks the southern edge and Lebo-hamath, verse 21, the far north, the entrance to the region of Hamath in Syria, the same northern limit named for Israel's borders in Numbers 34:8. Forty days was enough for a careful journey of that length and back.

Hebron receives special attention, verse 22. It was the place where Abraham lived and built an altar, Genesis 13:18, where Sarah died, Genesis 23:2, and where the patriarchs were buried. The narrator adds that it was built 'seven years before Zoan in Egypt.' Zoan was a city of the eastern Nile Delta, the region where God had worked wonders against Pharaoh, Psalm 78:12. The note quietly tells Israel that the city of their fathers is older than the Egyptian city they had known.

The spies came 'in the season for the first ripe grapes,' verse 20, which in the hill country is high summer. A single cluster carried on a pole between two men, verse 23, together with pomegranates and figs, was proof no one could deny.

The peoples listed in verse 29 match the land as it was: Amalekites in the Negev, where Israel had already met them in battle, Exodus 17:8; Hittites, Jebusites and Amorites in the hills; Canaanites on the coast and in the Jordan valley. The Anakim, verse 22, were remembered as a people of great stature, Deuteronomy 9:2. Forty years later Caleb would drive their three clans out of this very city, Joshua 15:14.
context.canonical:
The story of the spies is retold or recalled in almost every part of the Old Testament. Moses retells it in Deuteronomy 1:19-46 to the next generation, adding that the people themselves first proposed sending men ahead, Deuteronomy 1:22, and that 'in spite of all this, you did not trust the LORD your God,' Deuteronomy 1:32. He recalls it again in Numbers 32:8-13, when the tribes of Reuben and Gad seem about to repeat it by holding back from the land.

Joshua 14:6-14 closes the loop. Caleb, now eighty-five, reminds Joshua that he was forty when he was sent from Kadesh-barnea and 'brought back to him an honest report,' and he asks for Hebron, the very hill country of the Anakim that frightened the ten. Joshua 15:14 and Judges 1:20 record that he drove out the three sons of Anak named in Numbers 13:22.

Joshua 2 is a deliberate counterpart. Joshua sends two spies, not twelve, and they return with the report the ten should have given: 'the fear of you has fallen on us,' Joshua 2:9. The Canaanites had been more afraid of Israel than Israel was of them.

The Psalms turn the episode into a warning for worship. Psalm 106:24 sums it up: 'They despised the pleasant land; they did not believe His promise.' Psalm 95:7-11 is quoted and expounded at length in Hebrews 3:7-4:11, where the generation of Kadesh stands for anyone who hears God's promise and does not combine it with faith, Hebrews 4:2. Paul includes the wilderness generation among the examples 'written down as warnings for us,' 1 Corinthians 10:11, and Jude 1:5 reminds his readers that the Lord 'destroyed those who did not believe.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wrote this account for the generation that was about to stand where their parents had stood. They too would look across at fortified cities and tall peoples, Deuteronomy 9:1-2. The first purpose of the chapter is to show them exactly how the earlier failure happened, so that they would recognise it in themselves.

The chapter teaches them that faith and unbelief are not first of all a difference in information. The twelve went to the same places, carried the same fruit and saw the same people. What divided them was the reference point. The ten measured the Anakim against themselves and felt like grasshoppers. Caleb measured the land against the LORD's word, 'the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites,' verse 2, and concluded that the outcome was certain.

The chapter also warns about the power of a report. Leaders shape what a whole people believes about God. Ten representative men turned a balanced account into a campaign of discouragement, and the congregation followed them. Israel's leaders in every later generation were meant to hear that responsibility.

Finally, Moses wanted his readers to honour the one who stood alone. Caleb is from Judah, verse 6; later texts call him a Kenizzite, Numbers 32:12, a family that seems to have joined Israel from outside. The man who trusts is not the one with the most impressive pedigree but the one who takes God at His word.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a reconnaissance commanded for a particular moment. It does not teach that believers should never assess obstacles or gather facts. God Himself commanded the mission, and Moses' questions in verses 18 to 20 are sensible ones. Careful observation was never the sin.

What the chapter models, and later Scripture makes binding, is the posture from which facts are read. The ten did not lie about the fortified cities; their sin was the conclusion 'We cannot,' verse 31, drawn in the face of God's 'I am giving,' verse 2. Hebrews 3:12 turns that into a direct command: 'See to it, brothers, that none of you has a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God.'

Two cautions apply. The land of Canaan was a specific promise to a specific nation, so the passage does not guarantee believers success in any venture they choose to call God's will. And Caleb's courage was not self confidence; it rested on a promise already spoken. The application is to trust what God has actually said, not what we wish He had said.

debates.question: Who first proposed sending the spies, God or the people?

views.label: The accounts describe the same event from two angles
views.case: Numbers 13:1-2 records the LORD's command, while Deuteronomy 1:22-23 says the people asked for scouts and the plan seemed good to Moses. Many interpreters hold that the people proposed it, Moses brought it before the LORD, and God permitted and directed it. Numbers tells the story from the divine side, Deuteronomy from the human side, and Moses' sermon stresses the people's part because he is exposing their unbelief.

views.label: The request itself already betrayed hesitation
views.case: Others read the people's proposal in Deuteronomy 1:22 as a first sign of reluctance. God had already said the land was good, Exodus 3:8, and had told them to go up, Deuteronomy 1:21. On this view God granted the request as a test, the phrase 'send out for yourself' in Numbers 13:2 hinting that the mission was Israel's idea, allowed rather than initiated.

debates.bearing: Either way the mission was lawful, since it went out 'at the consent of the LORD,' verse 3. The failure lay not in sending spies but in refusing to believe what they found. Seeking information is never wrong; treating it as the final word over God's promise is.

debates.question: Were the ten spies wrong about the facts, or only about the conclusion?

views.label: Their facts were accurate but their conclusion faithless
views.case: Caleb never disputes that the cities are fortified or that the Anakim are there. Joshua 14:12 has him admit it forty years later. On this reading the chapter's lesson is that true facts, read without God, lead to false conclusions.

views.label: Their final report distorted the facts
views.case: Verse 32 calls their second account 'a bad report,' and its claims go beyond verse 28: the land that flowed with milk and honey now 'devours its inhabitants,' 'all the people' are giants, and the Anakim have become Nephilim. Fear did not only misread the evidence; it enlarged it. Numbers 14:36 calls it a report that made the congregation grumble.

debates.bearing: The text supports both, in sequence. Verses 27 to 29 are largely accurate; verses 32 and 33 are exaggerated. That movement is itself the warning: unbelief that starts by misreading facts soon begins to rewrite them.

study.originalLanguages:
Moses' instructions include a word that becomes important later. 'Be courageous,' verse 20, is a form of chazaq, to be strong or firm. It is the same root God will use when He tells Joshua three times, 'Be strong and courageous,' Joshua 1:6-9. The courage required of the spies is the courage later demanded of the conquest, and only two of the twelve showed it.

Caleb's words in verse 30 are emphatic in Hebrew in a way English struggles to carry. Both verbs are doubled with the infinitive, literally 'going up, let us go up,' and 'being able, we shall be able.' The BSB conveys the first with 'We must go up' and the second with 'we can certainly conquer it.' The ten answer with the same verb and a flat negative, 'We cannot,' verse 31, literally 'we are not able to go up.' The whole argument is a contest over one verb, able or not able.

The 'bad report' of verse 32 translates dibbah, a word for damaging talk, whispered and spread. It is the word used when Joseph brought his father 'a bad report' about his brothers, Genesis 37:2, and Proverbs 10:18 uses it for the one who 'spreads slander.' The spies' account became gossip against the land and, by implication, against the God who had called it good. Numbers 14:36-37 uses dibbah twice more for the report that set the congregation grumbling.

The claim that the land 'devours its inhabitants,' verse 32, uses the ordinary verb to eat. Ezekiel 36:13-14 picks up the same picture, 'You devour men,' and God promises that the land will no longer devour. What the ten meant as slander, God later turns into a promise to reverse.

The Nephilim of verse 33 appear elsewhere in Scripture only in Genesis 6:4, which describes 'the Nephilim' as 'on the earth in those days, and afterward as well.' By reaching for that word, the ten set the Anakim in the company of the pre-flood giants, the most frightening figures their tradition knew. 'Grasshoppers,' chagavim, is the word Isaiah 40:22 uses when he says that from God's throne 'its dwellers are like grasshoppers.' The ten were right about the scale; they simply forgot who is enthroned above it.

Two names carry weight. Eshcol means cluster, as the BSB footnote notes, so the valley is named for the fruit, verse 24. And Moses renames Hoshea, 'salvation,' as Joshua, Yehoshua, 'the LORD saves,' verse 16. In the Greek Old Testament his name is Iesous, the same form the New Testament uses for Jesus, and Hebrews 4:8 plays on the identity: 'if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day.'

typology.fulfillment: Moses gives Hoshea the name that means 'the LORD saves,' and the man who bears it stands with Caleb for the promise and later leads the next generation into the land. The angel gives the same name to Mary's son 'because He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21. The correspondence is intended by the name itself, and Hebrews 4:8 draws the line of escalation: Joshua led Israel into Canaan, but 'if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day.' The type falls short because Joshua could bring a people into a land but not into God's own rest; Jesus brings His people into both.

typology.type: The cluster of Eshcol, the firstfruits of the land brought back, Numbers 13:23
typology.fulfillment: The spies carried back a real portion of the inheritance before anyone had entered it, a foretaste that proved the promise true. The New Testament speaks of the Holy Spirit in the same terms: believers 'were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of our inheritance,' Ephesians 1:13-14. The escalation is that the Spirit is not a sample carried back by men but God Himself given to His people, and He cannot spoil as grapes do. The type also warns: the fruit was in Israel's hands, yet unbelief refused the land it came from. A foretaste without faith brings no one home.

typology.type: Caleb, the faithful witness of a 'different spirit,' Numbers 13:30 and 14:24
typology.fulfillment: Caleb stands almost alone for God's promise, is nearly stoned for it, and still receives the inheritance forty years later, Joshua 14:13. In this he points forward to the Faithful Witness, Revelation 1:5, who trusted the Father against the whole weight of human opinion and 'for the joy set before Him endured the cross,' Hebrews 12:2. The correspondence is real but partial. Caleb's faith was the faith of one sinner holding to a promise; Christ's faithfulness is the ground on which the promise itself stands, so that 'all the promises of God are Yes in Christ,' 2 Corinthians 1:20.

typology.type: The good land seen from its border, Numbers 13:27
typology.fulfillment: Israel saw the land and tasted its fruit but did not enter it. Hebrews 11:13 describes the patriarchs as having seen the promises 'and welcomed them from afar,' and Hebrews 4:1 warns 'while the promise of entering His rest still stands, let us be careful that none of you be deemed to have fallen short of it.' In Christ the inheritance is 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven,' 1 Peter 1:4. The type falls short because Canaan could be lost and was later lost again in exile; the inheritance Christ secures is kept by God for His people.

study.christ:
The line from this chapter to Christ does not run through an allegory of grapes or giants. It runs through the question the chapter itself asks: can God's people trust what He has promised when everything they see argues against it?

It begins with a name. Joshua, 'the LORD saves,' is one of only two spies who hold to the promise, and Matthew 1:21 gives Jesus that same name for the same reason. The first Joshua could bring a new generation into Canaan, but Hebrews 4:8-9 says that since he did not give them God's final rest, 'there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God.' The true Joshua leads His people into what Canaan only pictured.

The chapter's second link is the forty days, verse 25. Israel's forty days of looking at the land ended in the verdict 'We cannot.' Jesus, led by the Spirit into the wilderness 'for forty days,' Luke 4:1-2, faced the same testing that Israel failed and answered it from Deuteronomy 8:3, a verse written about the wilderness years: 'Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God,' Matthew 4:4. Where Israel measured God's word by the visible world, Jesus measured the visible world by God's word.

The third link is faithfulness. Caleb's confidence rested entirely on the words 'which I am giving,' verse 2. Paul says that 'all the promises of God are Yes in Christ,' 2 Corinthians 1:20. Christ is not only the one who believed God perfectly; He is the one in whom every promise is kept. John 8:29 records His own claim, 'I always do what pleases Him,' the opposite of the ten who tested God and would not listen.

There is also a contrast in the enemy. The Anakim and their fortified cities looked unbeatable, but they were still only men. The powers Christ faced were sin, death and the devil, which He overcame through His death and resurrection. That is why Romans 8:31 can ask, 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' and why 1 John 4:4 can say, 'greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world.' Believers are not called to imagine that the giants are small. They are called to remember who has already defeated the greatest enemy.

Finally, Christ is the answer to the grasshopper verdict. The ten saw themselves as tiny and concluded they were lost. The gospel agrees that we are small, and far weaker than we fear, and then announces that God's strength does not wait for ours. 'We are more than conquerors through Him who loved us,' Romans 8:37. Faith in this chapter is not bravado; it is confidence in another.
study.god:
The chapter opens with the LORD as the giver: 'the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites,' verse 2. The present participle matters. The gift is not a hope or an offer but something God is already doing. Everything that follows is a test of whether Israel will receive what God is already giving.

God is also the one who shows before He asks. He does not require Israel to march in blind. He sends men to see, lets them taste the fruit, and gives them forty days of evidence that He had told the truth about 'a land flowing with milk and honey,' Exodus 3:8. The ten spies themselves concede it, verse 27. God's promises are not a leap into the dark; He supplies reasons to trust Him, even while calling for trust beyond sight.

The chapter shows God's faithfulness to the patriarchs. Hebron, where Abraham built an altar and buried Sarah, is on the route, verse 22. The land God promised in Genesis 12:7 and Genesis 13:17 is still there, still good, still waiting. Genesis 15:16 had said that Israel would return 'in the fourth generation.' God has kept time.

It also shows that God's power does not depend on the odds. The size of the Anakim is not in doubt; the question is whether it matters. Deuteronomy 9:3 answers that 'the LORD your God goes across ahead of you as a consuming fire,' and Amos 2:9 recalls that God destroyed the Amorite 'though his height was like that of the cedars.' Isaiah 40:22 sets every people of the earth, giants included, as grasshoppers before His throne.

One more attribute sits quietly in the background: God's silence. After verse 2 He says nothing more in this chapter. He lets His word stand and lets the people answer. That restraint is not indifference. It is the dignity He gives to faith: He has spoken, and He waits to be believed.

There is a tension here that the chapter does not resolve on its own. God has promised the land, yet the generation that heard the promise will not enter it. The promise is sure, but its enjoyment is not automatic. God's faithfulness does not override unbelief; it outlasts it, and passes the promise to the children, Numbers 14:31.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to praise God for what He has said before they see it. Caleb's 'we can certainly conquer it' is a confession of faith in the God who gives. Every act of worship that says 'You are able' before the walls fall stands where Caleb stood.

crossReferences.note: Moses' own retelling adds details Numbers leaves out: the people first asked for spies, verse 22, the spies' report 'made our hearts melt,' verse 28, and above all 'in spite of all this, you did not trust the LORD your God,' verse 32. It names the root sin of Numbers 13 plainly.

Forty-five years later Caleb recalls that he was forty when he was sent from Kadesh-barnea and 'brought back to him an honest report.' At eighty-five he asks for the very hill country of the Anakim that terrified the ten. His faith has not aged.

Caleb drives out 'the three sons of Anak, the descendants of Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai,' the same three names the spies saw at Hebron in Numbers 13:22. The giants that ended one generation's hope become the trophy of one faithful man.

Rahab tells Joshua's spies that 'all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of you.' The Canaanites had been terrified of Israel all along. The report of Joshua 2 is the one the ten spies failed to bring back, and it shows how fear had blinded them.

The only other mention of the Nephilim in Scripture, describing the mighty men of old before the flood. The ten spies invoke that ancient and terrifying name in Numbers 13:33 to turn the Anakim into something more than men, which is fear reaching for the darkest words it can find.

Isaiah uses the spies' own image of grasshoppers, but from the other end: from God's throne 'its dwellers are like grasshoppers.' The spies felt small before the Anakim; Isaiah reminds Israel that the Anakim and all nations are small before God.

The psalm's verdict on Kadesh: 'They despised the pleasant land; they did not believe His promise. They grumbled in their tents.' It names the spies' report as contempt for God's gift, not merely caution, and ties the land's rejection to the rejection of His word.

The writer applies the whole episode to the church. 'See to it, brothers, that none of you has a wicked heart of unbelief,' and concludes 'it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter.' Numbers 13 is where that unbelief first spoke aloud.

The message the Kadesh generation heard 'was of no value to them, since they did not share the faith of those who comprehended it.' The promise was the same for Caleb and for the ten; the difference was faith. The writer urges readers not to fall short of the rest that still stands open.

Moses warns the tribes of Reuben and Gad that holding back from the land would repeat what 'your fathers did when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea.' It shows that the spies' failure became Israel's standing warning, recalled whenever a new reluctance appeared.

Abraham faced the fact of his aged body and Sarah's barren womb, yet 'did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God,' being 'fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised.' It is the exact posture of Caleb and the exact opposite of the ten.

Mary's son is given the name Jesus 'because He will save His people from their sins.' It is the name Moses gave Hoshea in Numbers 13:16, the LORD saves, now given to the one who will bring God's people into the rest the first Joshua could not give.

study.oneStory:
In creation God gave humanity a good place to live and to rule, a garden 'very good,' Genesis 1:31. In the fall that place was lost, and ever since the question has been whether and how God would bring His people home. The promise to Abraham, 'I will give this land to your offspring,' Genesis 12:7, was the first concrete answer. The exodus set it in motion. Numbers 13 brings the story to the very edge of its fulfilment.

What happens there repeats the fall in a new form. Eden was lost when the first couple doubted that God's word was good and true. At Kadesh a nation hears again that the land is good, sees it with its own eyes, and then doubts that God can be trusted to give it. The pattern of Genesis 3, a word of God questioned and a gift refused, is the pattern of Numbers 13.

The chapter sets up much of what follows. It explains the forty years, the death of a generation, and the reason Deuteronomy must be preached again on the plains of Moab. It gives Caleb and Joshua their place in the story, and Joshua 21:43-45 later closes the circle: 'Not one of all the LORD's good promises to the house of Israel had failed.'

Yet Canaan was never the end of the story. Israel would possess the land and later lose it in exile. Psalm 95 was sung long after the conquest, still warning, 'Today, if you hear His voice,' and Hebrews 4:8-9 draws the conclusion that the rest Joshua gave was not the final one. The land becomes a picture of a greater inheritance.

In Christ that inheritance comes into view. The true Joshua has passed through the testing where Israel fell. His Spirit is the cluster from Eshcol, a real foretaste carried back to those still on the road. The church stands, as Israel stood, between promise and possession, and it hears the same call to believe.

The story ends not at a border but in a city. Revelation 21:1-4 shows a new heaven and a new earth where 'the dwelling place of God is with man.' The land that 'devours its inhabitants' in the spies' slander gives way to a world with 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain.' And the giants that made Israel feel like grasshoppers are nowhere to be found, because every enemy has been put under the feet of the One who went in first.

sermon.title: Fear, Faith and Courage
sermon.why: Preached on Numbers 13-14, Keller explores how biblical courage is inseparable from faith, showing that the ultimate fear behind Israel's unbelief was a mistrust in God, and that true security is found only in resting completely on Him.

questions: Ten spies and Caleb saw the exact same land, the exact same obstacles, yet reached completely opposite conclusions. What situation in your life are you currently viewing through fear rather than through the lens of God's proven faithfulness?

The ten spies' report contained real facts but was ultimately faithless in its conclusion, we cannot. How do you distinguish between honestly acknowledging a difficulty and using that difficulty as an excuse for unbelief?

Caleb stood almost entirely alone against the majority's fear, trusting God's promise over the crowd's consensus. Where do you need the courage to hold a minority position of faith, even when most around you are moving toward fear or compromise?

The spies described themselves as grasshoppers compared to the land's inhabitants, a self-image that shaped their entire outlook. How does your view of yourself, rather than your view of God, sometimes determine whether you step forward in faith or shrink back in fear?

This whole episode is remembered in the New Testament as a direct warning against hardening your heart in unbelief. What promise of God are you currently at risk of doubting because the obstacle in front of you looks too large?

translationNotes.note: Moses gave to Hoshea son of Nun the name Joshua marks a significant renaming, from Hoshea, meaning salvation, to Joshua, meaning the LORD saves, foreshadowing his future role leading Israel into the land.
It had been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt is an editorial aside comparing Hebron's antiquity to a well-known Egyptian city, likely added for readers familiar with Egyptian chronology.

The Nephilim, mentioned earlier in Genesis 6:4, are invoked here to heighten the sense of overwhelming, almost legendary opposition; whether this is an accurate identification or fear-driven exaggeration is debated among interpreters.
